claims.text: Replacing a conventional EAM reference with an HDNNP trained on solid and liquid ab initio configurations near melting will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The HDNNP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by more than 50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
A diverse ab initio training set can cover configurations from both solid and liquid high-temperature phases.
The proposed training set spans the many-body interactions present in both phases.
The method is applicable to equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys, including systems similar to high-entropy carbonitrides.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 50–100 K below or above the melting point.
The trained neural-network potential can accurately represent solid, liquid, and disordered configurations in a high-entropy carbonitride.
The HDNNP captures the full spectrum of local atomic environments and many-body interactions.
Capturing this broader spectrum of environments improves phase-space overlap with the ab initio target.
Rigid EAM potentials fail to reproduce the diversity of configurations in the ab initio liquid.
Improved phase-space overlap reduces discrepancies along the thermodynamic-integration path.
The resulting free-energy benchmarks will be closer to ab initio predictions than benchmarks obtained with EAM references.
TOR-TILD's conventional EAM references exhibit considerable integration-path mismatch because they inadequately sample the ab initio configurational space.
The benefit may not occur for compositions far from equiatomic ratios.
The benefit may not occur at temperatures outside the stated 50–100 K window around melting.
Evidence from elemental and binary systems supports the expected improvement.
The exact reduction in path mismatch may depend on alloy system and training-set quality.
A parallel comparison against the TOR-TILD EAM reference can test the HDNNP using free-energy differences, path convergence, and phase-space-overlap metrics.
Failure to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by at least 50% relative to the EAM reference falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires a reduction of more than 50%, whereas the falsification rule treats a reduction of exactly 50% as sufficient because it requires at least 50%.
